newsitem.title: USA: POLL - Fed seen lifting rates once more in 1997.
newsitem.headline: POLL - Fed seen lifting rates once more in 1997.

text.p: Official short-term interest rates in the United States will rise once in the second half of 1997, peak in early 1998 and slowly trend lower again until they return to current levels by mid-1999, economists said in the latest Reuters quarterly economic survey.

Thirty-three forecasters at banks, securities firms and research institutions offered a median projection for a 5.75 percent Federal funds rate in the second half of 1997 that would rise to six percent in the first quarter of 1998.
Higher rates would eventually cool economic growth enough to allow the Federal Reserve to let the funds rate fall back to 5.75 percent for the remainder of 1998 and early 1999.
The economists' median projection for the Federal funds rate in the second quarter of 1999 was 5.50 percent, the Fed's current target for the rate.
Maria Fiorini Ramirez, president of MFR Inc, was on the low side of the average (mean) forecasts of Fed funds in the second half of 1997 and through 1998.
The poll's mean Fed funds rate forecasts were 5.63 percent in the third quarter of 1997 and 5.83 percent in the fourth.
In 1998, the mean Fed funds forecasts were 5.94 percent in the first quarter of 1998, 5.91 percent in the second quarter, 5.87 percent in the third, and 5.78 percent in the fourth.
In a moderate contrast, Ramirez expects the Fed to push the funds rate to 5.75 percent in the second half of 1997 and to keep it there through 1998.
"We think there will be some economic rebound in the second half of the year and the Fed could tighten by 25 basis points before year-end, but we don't expect more than that," she said.
Even that 25-basis-point hike is not certain, she said.

"We think the economy has underlying strength but inflation is low," she said. "We think there's going to be a long period of stable monetary policy. Whether the funds rate will be 5-1/2 percent or 5-3/4 percent is very fifty-fifty."

Robert Brusca, chief economist with The Nikko Securities Co International Inc, expects the Fed funds rate to rise to 5.75 percent in September and to six percent in the fourth quarter. There it would remain until the economy cools and the Fed sees fit to lower it to 5.75 percent in the third quarter of 1998 and to 5.50 percent in the last quarter of the year.

In a press briefing on Tuesday, Brusca said the U.S. inventory cycle would turn up in the second half of 1997 and that the risks of inflation had worsened. The Fed is wary of the low 5.0 percent unemployment rate and firm money and credit growth, Brusca said. Meanwhile, renewed consumer spending in the latter half of the year will spur the economy's growth, a condition that will cause the Fed to hike rates later in 1997, Brusca said.
Chris Rupkey, vice president and financial economist at Bank of Tokyo Mitsubishi, said he is looking for rate hikes totaling 50 basis points.
"I call a halt at six percent," he said. "It's hard to forecast a string of Fed tightenings because there's simply no inflation."
Ramirez concurred.

"We believed early in the year that inflation was not going to be a problem and that the Fed would not tighten three or four times (as some economists forecast) because it wasn't needed and we still think that's pretty much the case," she said.
"The Fed is way ahead of the inflation curve," said Rupkey.
The Reuters Poll was conducted July 7-9.
Additional inquiries should be directed to Jeff Coelho, 212-859-1562.
